Former councillor calls for town bus service at Musselburgh

3 hrs ago
Transport
Musselburgh
By Avril Campbell Reporter

Share

0 comments
0:00 / 0:00

The need for a town bus service in Musselburgh has been highlighted by a local resident and former councillor.

Barry Turner, who lives at Inveresk, claimed that, as the town has grown, some of the new developments on the fringe were not well served by buses.

He said: “Much is proposed in Musselburgh in respect of provision for active travel, that is walking, cycling and - if legal - wheeling. But what about the less active who may not have access to a car or who may prefer not to use the car given levels of congestion and difficulties with parking?”

“There has been little or no investment in bus services as the town grows substantially and some of the new developments on the fringe are not well served by buses which tend to be concentrated on the routes into Edinburgh.”

Mr Turner explained: “Some years ago there was an SMT bus running between Wallyford and Stoneyhill. It was withdrawn. More recently there was the Tesco bus linking residential areas with the store which only a few bus routes actually serve. It was withdrawn. There is a case for bringing back a local town service complementing the active travel proposals and helping to reduce car dependency.”

“I suspect that such a service would need to be supported financially by East Lothian Council in the way it supports a number of bus services across the county. It could serve the High Streets, the supermarkets, the health centre and the station. It would link these through dedicated local provision, unaffected by congestion elsewhere, with established, new and proposed housing areas.

“In particular, the expanding Monktonhall/Old Craighall area is in dire need of a more regular service and the Edenhall Hospital site, remote from a bus route, will need a bus up Edenhall Road when redeveloped. There used to be one but it was withdrawn as was a link into The Muckletts.”

And he added: “Overall I think there is a challenge here for the incoming council next year, that is if nothing can be done beforehand.”

An East Lothian Council spokesperson said that the local authority recognised the important role that public transport played in supporting residents who travelled by bus, did not have access to a car, or were unable to walk or cycle.

"While active travel remains an important part of the council's transport strategy, we will continue to work with operators and partners to maintain and improve public transport provision where possible," said the spokesperson.

“The council invests significantly in supported bus services. However, this funding must be prioritised towards communities that would otherwise have little or no access to public transport. A number of rural settlements across East Lothian rely on council-supported services to provide access to employment, education, healthcare and essential services where commercial operators are unable to operate viable routes."

Musselburgh was, in contrast, one of the "best-served areas in East Lothian in terms of public transport provision", said the council.

" The town is currently served by 18 bus services operated by a number of commercial providers," explained the spokesperson.

"These services not only provide direct links to destinations such as Edinburgh, Haddington, Tranent, Prestonpans and North Berwick, but also offer excellent interchange opportunities, allowing passengers to connect to a much wider network across East Lothian, Edinburgh and beyond.

“Given the level of existing provision in Musselburgh and the budget available to the council, it is currently not possible to provide additional supported service funding for the town when other communities in East Lothian are either dependent upon council-supported services to meet essential travel needs or presently have little or no access to public transport.

“We appreciate the points raised regarding accessibility to specific destinations, particularly for residents in newer housing developments and areas not located directly on existing bus corridors. The council continues to monitor population growth, development proposals and changing travel patterns, and will continue to engage with operators, developers and regional partners to identify opportunities to improve connectivity where there is evidence of need and demand.

“In relation to the former Tesco bus service, it is worth noting this was operated through a private commercial arrangement between Tesco and Horsburgh Travel rather than being a council-supported service. The decision to withdraw the service therefore rested with those organisations and was not a result of council funding decisions.”
